summary: Describes an extension to the MPLS LSP echo request that lets a BFD system ask the egress peer to use a specific path for the reverse direction of a BFD session when monitoring an explicit unidirectional path. The status is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: To check a one-way road, you also need to say which road the answer should take back. This adds that request.

subtitle: Specify the return path for failure detection on one-way MPLS tunnels.

tldr.problem: When BFD monitors a unidirectional MPLS tunnel, the return path for BFD control packets may differ from the monitored forward path, leading to false failure alarms from problems on the reverse path rather than the tunnel being monitored.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a new TLV (Type-Length-Value field) that can be included in MPLS LSP echo requests to instruct the remote end to use a specific path for its BFD control packet responses, creating a symmetric bidirectional path.
tldr.outcome: BFD can now monitor traffic-engineered unidirectional paths more accurately by ensuring both directions use co-routed paths, reducing false alarms and improving failure detection reliability.

today: RFC 9612 is an Experimental specification published in July 2024. It provides an optional mechanism for operators who want to improve BFD accuracy on traffic-engineered MPLS tunnels and has been developed based on operational experience from real deployments.

sections.title: Monitoring Unidirectional Paths
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is used to quickly detect failures in network paths. However, when BFD monitors a traffic-engineered unidirectional MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP), there is a fundamental asymmetry: the forward direction follows the engineered path specified by the network operator, but the return direction for BFD responses typically follows the shortest path computed by normal routing protocols.

This asymmetry creates a problem: if a failure occurs on the reverse path (but not on the monitored forward path), BFD will detect it and incorrectly report a failure on the tunnel, even though the actual data path is working. This RFC extends the MPLS LSP echo request mechanism to allow the ingress router to instruct the egress router to send BFD control packets back along a specified path, typically the reverse of the forward path.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a letter and want to know if the road was safe, you also need to make sure the reply comes back the same way.

sections.title: The Problem of Asymmetric Paths
sections.content:
MPLS allows network operators to explicitly engineer paths for traffic using Label Switched Paths (LSPs). When BFD monitors such an engineered LSP in the forward direction, it sends BFD control packets in-band using the same path as the monitored traffic. However, unless explicitly configured, the responses return via standard IP routing, which may choose a completely different path.

This path asymmetry introduces false positive BFD notifications. A link failure on the return path, unrelated to the engineered forward tunnel, will cause BFD to incorrectly declare the monitored path as failed. By ensuring both directions use congruent (matching) paths, the potential for such false alarms is greatly reduced, and operators can be confident that BFD failures truly reflect problems with the monitored path.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a one-way street for data going out. If the answer comes back a different way and that way breaks, you'd think your one-way street broke.

sections.title: The BFD Reverse Path TLV
sections.content:
This RFC defines a new TLV type 16384 to carry information about the reverse path. The TLV contains sub-TLVs that describe the path the egress router should use for BFD responses. Only non-multicast Target Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) Stack sub-TLVs are permitted, as multicast paths are not supported for BFD reverse paths.

The TLV is optional but, when used, must accompany the BFD Discriminator TLV in an LSP echo request. If the receiving router cannot find the specified reverse path or encounters invalid sub-TLVs, it returns a specific error code. An empty BFD Reverse Path TLV serves as a withdrawal signal, instructing the egress to revert to its default behavior of using standard routing for responses.
sections.plainLanguage: A tiny instruction tag that says 'send answers back this specific way' instead of 'the usual way'.

sections.title: How It Works: An Example
sections.content:
Consider an ingress router A that wants to monitor two separate engineered tunnels to an egress router H. It can bootstrap one BFD session to monitor the A-B-C-D-G-H path by including a BFD Reverse Path TLV that specifies the reverse path H-G-D-C-B-A. Simultaneously, it can set up another BFD session for the A-B-E-F-G-H path with a reverse path of H-G-F-E-B-A.

Each BFD session identified by its BFD Discriminator value has an associated reverse path specified in the Reverse Path TLV. When the egress router receives BFD control packets for these sessions, it forwards the responses along the specified paths rather than using default routing. If the egress router later detects a path failure, it can initiate a new BFD session in the opposite direction by looking up the reverse path information in its state.
sections.plainLanguage: You can set up multiple one-way paths and tell each one exactly which way to send answers back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The BFD Reverse Path TLV could be exploited by including an excessive number of sub-TLVs, which might consume server resources. To mitigate this threat, the default limit is set to 128 sub-TLV entries per Reverse Path TLV, though implementations may allow operators to configure this limit. Additionally, security considerations from the underlying BFD and MPLS protocols (RFCs 5880, 5884, 7726, and 8029) apply to this extension.

Operators should apply the same security practices for configuring reverse paths as for configuring the forward paths being monitored, ensuring that only authorized operators can modify the paths that BFD uses for bidirectional monitoring.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could try to send too many instructions to slow things down, so there's a limit on how many are allowed.
